A content delivery network solves a simple problem: when many people in different places ask for the same website content at once, a single distant computer answering every request gets slow. Instead, copies of that content sit on many computers spread around the world, so each request travels a shorter distance.

Here is how the pieces fit together. The origin server is the original computer where the website's content first lives — the master copy. An edge location is one of many smaller stations placed closer to where people actually are, each holding a copy of that content. When someone requests a page and the nearest edge location already has a saved copy ready to hand over, that is called a cache hit — no need to contact the original computer at all.

Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries selling loaves baked at one central factory: instead of everyone driving across town to the factory, each bakery keeps fresh loaves on hand, so most people get bread from the shop around the corner. Only when a bakery runs out does someone fetch more from the factory. That is the essence of the system: distributing copies close to demand, so delivery is fast, and reserving trips to the original source for when nearby copies are missing or outdated.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing the real, master content | Everything ultimately comes from here if no copy exists nearby |
| Edge location | A nearby station holding a copy of the content | Shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered instantly from a saved copy | Means faster loading and less strain on the origin |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and reliable no matter where a request comes from |
